notes_context:
Memory items from past tasks:
- [rb-0001] Round money with the project's round_money helper: Monetary results must be rounded via ledgerly.money.round_money (half-up to the cent), not Python's round() or bare Decimal.quantize(), which use banker's rounding.
  Before returning any computed money value, wrap it in the repository's round_money helper. Check ledgerly/money.py for the canonical rounding function and reuse it so invoice totals match finance expectations.
- [rb-0002] Read the money module before implementing money math: Inspecting ledgerly/money.py and existing invoice functions (line_total, invoice_total) reveals the required helpers and conventions.
  When adding a money-related function, first read the money module and sibling functions to learn available helpers (to_money, round_money, ZERO) and the established pattern of converting inputs then rounding outputs.
- [rb-0003] Handle empty/zero-denominator cases explicitly: Guard against division by zero by returning the module's ZERO constant when total quantity is zero.
  Compute the denominator first and return ZERO (the project's zero-money constant) when it is zero, rather than relying on exception handling or returning a plain int 0.
- [rb-0004] Mirror sibling-module validation patterns: Before implementing a new function, grep sibling modules for existing error codes and validation idioms and reuse them.
  Search the package for BillingError raises and isinstance checks to learn the project's conventions (e.g. rejecting bool before int, using to_money/round_money for amounts). Matching those patterns makes hidden tests pass and keeps behavior consistent.
- [rb-0005] Read the target test file and models first: Inspect the dedicated test file, dataclasses, and error class before writing code so signatures and field names match exactly.
  Check models.py for the exact LineItem/Invoice fields and status values, and tests/test_*.py for expected error codes and return values. This avoids guessing attribute names or status strings.
- [rb-0006] Guard bools when validating integers: Python treats bool as an int subclass, so explicitly reject bool before isinstance(x, int) checks.
  When validating a positive integer parameter, write `isinstance(x, bool) or not isinstance(x, int) or x <= 0` to raise the invalid-input error. Also normalize money inputs through the project's to_money/round_money helpers before comparing to ZERO.

review_comments: [team convention] Money in ledgerly is Decimal end-to-end and always has exactly two decimal places. Never convert amounts to float.

item.title: Reuse existing money helpers instead of raw Decimal math
item.description: The repo already provides to_money/round_money in ledgerly/money.py that enforce Decimal-only, two-decimal money; use them rather than reimplementing conversion or rounding.
item.content: Before writing money logic, grep for existing helpers (to_money, round_money, ZERO, CENT) and error types (BillingError with code+message). Compose new functions from them so rounding policy and float rejection stay consistent across the codebase.

item.title: Convert rates via Decimal(str(value)), never float arithmetic
item.description: Tax rates may arrive as int/float/str; converting through str into Decimal avoids float contamination while still accepting common inputs.
item.content: Write a small _to_rate helper: reject bools, pass Decimal through, and for int/float/str use Decimal(str(value)) catching InvalidOperation to raise the project's BillingError. Then do all percentage math in Decimal (rate / Decimal('100')).

item.title: Validate ranges with Decimal comparisons and project error codes
item.description: Range checks like 0 <= rate <= 100 should be done on the Decimal value and raise BillingError with a machine-readable code, matching sibling modules' style.
item.content: After conversion, compare with Decimal bounds (e.g. Decimal('0') <= rate <= Decimal('100')) and raise BillingError('invalid_rate', repr(original)) on failure. Mirror the code/message conventions seen in clock.py, invoice.py, and money.py.
